analysis: Warfarin is an anticoagulant that works by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, including factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S. The use of warfarin can lead to a paradoxical increase in clotting risk during the initial phase of treatment due to the rapid depletion of protein C, which has a shorter half-life than many clotting factors. This can result in skin necrosis, particularly in individuals with underlying deficiencies in protein C or protein S. Among the options provided, protein C deficiency is the most directly associated with warfarin-induced skin necrosis due to its role in the regulation of coagulation and the fact that its depletion can lead to thrombosis and subsequent skin necrosis. Protein S deficiency can also contribute to similar outcomes, but the classic association is stronger with protein C deficiency. Hemophilia and antithrombin III deficiency are not typically associated with warfarin-induced skin necrosis. Therefore, the best-supported option is protein C deficiency.
